title: An Innovative Hunting-based Quantum-inspired Jaguar Algorithm for Combinatorial Optimization
journal_or_venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE)
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a quantum-inspired Jaguar algorithm (QJA) that embeds the hunting mechanism from the classical Jaguar algorithm into quantum-inspired optimization to adaptively adjust convergence in the superposition state for combinatorial problems. Evaluated on real-world portfolio optimization (TSX top 30), QJA converges faster and yields higher-quality portfolios compared with other QIO methods such as QTS and GQTS.
methodology_description: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-inspired Jaguar Algorithm (QJA) for combinatorial optimization, integrating the Jaguar Algorithm's hunting mechanism into a quantum-inspired optimization framework. Each solution is represented as a vector of qubit-like superposition states initialized to equal probability (|ψ_i> = 1/sqrt(2)(|0>+|1>)). A measurement maps each qubit to a binary decision (select stock or not) with Pr(|1>) determined by the state's amplitude. Fitness is evaluated using a Trend Ratio (Expected Return / Risk). The update rule adjusts each bit probability b_i toward the global best (sgb) and away from the local worst (slw): b_i <- b_i ± θ depending on sgb_i and slw_i. A hunting-based adaptive mechanism adjusts θ dynamically (initial θ = 2^-24 relative to 0.5) by doubling or halving it based on the historical flips/consistency between sgb and slw across successive iterations to accelerate when a clear tendency is detected and decelerate when the environment is indistinguishable or divergent. QJA inherits the QTS concept of approaching the best while avoiding the worst. The algorithm is evaluated on a portfolio optimization task and compared to QTS and GQTS baselines across sliding windows.
dataset_used: Top 30 companies by market capitalization on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX), time span 2013–2022, training-to-testing period total reported as 831 (sliding-window evaluation). Initial virtual fund: $10,000,000.
experiment_input: Source: Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) top 30 by market value. Size: 30 assets, historical data spanning 2013–2022 with a reported total period length of 831 (used in sliding-window training/testing). Preprocessing: not detailed in the paper (no specific data cleaning, feature engineering, or return calculation steps provided).
experiment_process: Pipeline: (1) Initialize each particle's superposition states to equal probability. (2) Measure superpositions to produce binary portfolio selections (bit = 1 means include asset). (3) Evaluate portfolio fitness using Trend Ratio = Expected Return / Risk. (4) Identify global best (sgb) and local worst (slw). (5) Update per-bit probabilities b_i via b_i <- b_i + θ if sgb_i=1 & slw_i=0; b_i <- b_i - θ if sgb_i=0 & slw_i=1; else no change. (6) Adapt θ using hunting rules: start θ = 2^-24 (relative to 0.5) and double or halve θ based on changes between previous and current sgb/slw states (doubling on clear convergence tendency, halving on indistinguishable or divergent tendencies). (7) Repeat measurement/update loop for 10,000 iterations. (8) Perform 50 independent runs and evaluate across sliding windows; compare results against QTS and GQTS baselines. Parameters explicitly reported: iterations=10,000, runs=50, initial θ=2^-24, assets=30, initial fund $10M.
experiment_output: Output metrics: Trend Ratio (Expected Return / Risk) reported per sliding window and averaged; #Opt (count of optimal occurrences) per method; percentage improvement over baselines. Results presented as numeric tables of Trend Ratio and #Opt, percentage improvement, average over 831 windows, and convergence plots showing objective vs iterations. Baselines: QTS and GQTS.

results_summary: The paper introduces QJA, a quantum-inspired algorithm incorporating the Jaguar Algorithm's hunting-based adaptive update (doubling/halving of θ) into a superposition-based QIO framework. On a real-world financial testbed (top 30 TSX stocks, 831 sliding windows across 2013–2022), with 10,000 iterations and 50 independent runs, QJA achieved higher average Trend Ratio and robustness than two baselines (QTS and GQTS). Quantitatively, QJA's average Trend Ratio over all windows was 0.290984974 versus 0.252402722 for QTS (reported 13.26% improvement), and convergence plots indicate QJA reaches higher-quality solutions earlier in the search. The authors argue these gains come from the hunting-based adaptive θ adjustments, transferring JA's exploitation/exploration mechanism into a quantum-inspired setting.
